content: AD-36 is one of the 51 known types of adenoviruses that can infect humans. It was first identified as being associated with obesity in chickens by Dr. Nikhil Dhurandhar. Research has demonstrated a positive correlation between the presence of AD-36 antibodies in the blood and increased body fat in humans. Experimental studies have shown that animals, such as chickens and mice, injected with similar adenoviruses exhibit statistically significant weight gain. In some cases, the test subjects experienced a 2.5-fold increase in fat storage. A unique characteristic of the weight gain associated with AD-36 is the absence or markedly low levels of lipids, triglycerides, and cholesterol in the blood of affected individuals. This is in contrast to typical obesity, where these substances are usually elevated in the bloodstream as part of the metabolic process. The current hypothesis suggests that these chemicals are being stored within cells rather than circulating in the blood, although the exact mechanism remains unknown. AD-36 has been shown to increase fat accumulation in chickens and other non-human subjects. However, it is important to note that AD-36 is not considered the sole or primary cause of obesity. While it has been proven to induce fat gain, the duration and long-term effects of this phenomenon are not well understood. Further studies have been conducted on other human adenoviruses, such as AD-37 and AD-2. AD-37 was found to have a similar effect on fat tissue, as it promoted the differentiation of human stem cells into fat cells. However, unlike AD-36, AD-37 caused an increase in cholesterol levels. In contrast, AD-2 demonstrated the opposite effect, as it was observed to reduce body fat in test subjects. The most significant findings from these experiments, conducted in 2004 for AD-36 and in 2007 for AD-37, highlight the complex and varied effects of different adenoviruses on fat metabolism. It is crucial to emphasize that adenoviruses are not the sole contributors to obesity, and further research is necessary to determine whether they play a role in long-term obesity development.
